newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania plans to slash budget deficit in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Romania plans to slash budget deficit in 1997.

text.p: Romania's government released its draft budget on Monday calling for a big reduction in the deficit and officials said tough austerity measures lay ahead to meet ambitious targets.
The draft provides for the budget deficit to be reduced to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from last year's 5.8 percent, in line with guidelines from the International Monetary Fund.
"The biggest difficulty will be to slash the consolidated budget deficit to 4.5 percent. This calls for tremendous effort," a senior government source said.
"The budget deficit has a big influence on inflation and the foreign trade deficit. We are in control of the situation. At no time will the Romanian economy slip from our control."
A copy of the budget made available to Reuters put 1997 budget revenues at around 70.4 trillion lei, with spending at some 80.9 trillion lei, yielding a deficit of 10.5 trillion.
It gave no dollar equivalents for budget figures.
Romania's leu currency has been subject to sharp fluctuations in recent weeks. It was quoted on Monday on the interbank market at about 9,100 against the dollar, compared with 4,100 in the New Year.
The draft has yet to be discussed in a government meeting and then to be submitted for approval to parliament, where the government's centre-right allies hold a comfortable majority.

Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea's government -- which came to power after leftists were defeated in last November's election - is committed to capping deficits after long talks last month with the IMF and World Bank.
But it has also pledged to look after Romanians thrown into poverty after little progress on reform since the 1989 fall of communism. About 10 percent of GDP is earmarked for social security.

The government's figures apply to the "consolidated budget", which includes the state budget, local government budgets, social security expenditure, supplementary pension funds and various other extra-budgetary funds.
The bulk of 1997 consolidated revenues comes from profit and wage taxes, which total 40.2 trillion lei.

Ciorbea last week said removing tax holidays and raising excise duties on alcohol and tobacco would boost revenues. But he said funds from planned privatisations had not been considered when drafting the budget.
Subsidies to bloated communist-era industry have been halved, with capital spending falling 17 percent. Capital spending under the draft stood at 9.3 trillion lei.
Both the IMF and World Bank withheld credits for Romania last year due to foreign exchange market curbs and the overshooting of spending targets.
Last year's deficit figure of 5.8 percent of GDP was nearly three times greater than an IMF-agreed target.
Officials estimate year-on-year inflation this year at 89.5 percent against 56.9 percent in 1996 -- boosted by price liberalisation for fuel, electricity and food.
They also forecast negative growth in the first half at least.
Ciorbea said the bulk of the consolidated budget gap -- about 3.4 percent -- would be financed through external credits. The rest would be funded by domestic loans.
Romania is seeking around $1 billion in total loans from the IMF and World Bank to underpin its tough reforms.
